result: Variations in loading history affect fingertip deformation in a viscoelastic manner. In regular sequences, contactor paths were consistent across trials, but showed hysteresis, creep, and anisotropic deviations. In irregular sequences, contactor paths varied markedly depending on previous loading direction, with variability 20× greater at force onset, 7× during plateau, and 4× at retraction end, indicating persistent viscoelastic memory effects.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm these mechanical findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the data and analyses are compelling' regarding viscoelastic effects on skin mechanics. Reviewer 2 notes 'there is a clear effect of viscoelasticity on the imposed skin movements from a force-controlled stimulus' and praises the 'elegant design' with 'accurate measurements of global skin mechanics.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'viscoelasticity was shown to affect the mechanical skin deflections.'

result: Variations in loading history reduced neural information about current force direction across all three neuron types. Firing rate variability during force protraction was 2× higher for FA-1, nearly 2× for SA-1, and 70% higher for SA-2 neurons in irregular vs. regular sequences. Information accumulation rates were considerably lower and plateaued at lower values in irregular sequences, with effects most prominent during force protraction.
evaluation: Reviewers unanimously support these findings. Reviewer 1 describes the study as investigating 'whether and to what extent the previous applied force directions impact the firing' and states the data are 'compelling.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'both skin mechanics and evoked afferent firing were affected based on prior stimulation' and notes 'the result of this was an impaired coding of contact forces.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors have succeeded in demonstrating skin viscoelasticity has an impact...on the resultant neural coding of force.'

result: Individual neurons showed heterogeneous responses to loading history. Most neurons (46 SA-1, 35 FA-1, 18 SA-2) primarily signaled current force direction, while minorities showed mixed tuning or primarily signaled preceding direction. Information about preceding direction was present early in protraction (60-70ms), and even 'current-tuned' FA-1 and SA-1 neurons showed reduced information transmission in irregular sequences. This diversity suggests population-level encoding of viscoelastic state containing memory of past stimulation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall demonstration of viscoelastic effects. Reviewer 2 specifically notes the study reveals 'dynamic coding properties' and praises the 'advanced analysis method...applied to a large dataset to study neural encoding of force, the temporal dynamics of this, and the variability in this.' The heterogeneity findings are implicitly accepted as reviewers affirm the overall conclusions without questioning the neuron classification or diversity claims.

result: SA-2 neurons with ongoing activity (20/41) signaled information about the fingertip's viscoelastic state during interstimulus periods when unloaded. Population analysis showed good match between neural representation and fingertip deformation, with trial types clustered by preceding force direction throughout interstimulus periods, then transitioning to cluster by current direction during protraction.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support SA-2 findings. Reviewer 2 notes 'it is particularly noteworthy that the SA-2s have been thoroughly analyzed and play an important role here' and states the manuscript is 'well-presented.' Reviewer 3 confirms the study demonstrates effects on 'the resultant neuronal signalling' without raising concerns about SA-2-specific claims. The thorough SA-2 analysis is treated as a strength rather than questioned.

result: Regression modeling showed neuronal firing is determined by fingertip deformation rather than applied force. Two-way interaction models (position × velocity) achieved R² of 0.75 (FA-1), 0.88 (SA-1), 0.91 (SA-2). Variable importance and prediction accuracy varied across neurons of the same type. SA-2 neurons showed highest prediction accuracy, consistent with contactor behavior reflecting bulk deformation; lower accuracy for SA-1 and FA-1 suggests influence of additional factors like partial slips.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these analytical findings. Reviewer 2 praises the 'analytical techniques used' and notes 'analysis of fundamental information coding and information representation in the sensory afferents reveals dynamic coding properties.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors have succeeded in demonstrating skin viscoelasticity has an impact on skin contact mechanics with a given force and that this impacts on the resultant neural coding' and confirms 'their study has been well designed and the results support their conclusions.'

result: Differences between neuron types in sensitivity to loading history were observed. FA-1 and SA-1 showed more pronounced history effects than SA-2 during force protraction. This may relate to Type I neurons sensing fingerprint ridge deformation (susceptible to partial slips) while SA-2 neurons sense deeper tissue tension states (reflecting bulk deformation).
evaluation: Reviewers accept these neuron-type differences as part of the overall findings. Reviewer 1 notes the study examined 'the firing of FA-1, SA-1 and SA-2 neurons' and found effects differed between types. Reviewer 2 confirms 'a clear effect of recent physical skin state (memory), which is different between afferents.' The mechanistic explanations based on known receptor properties are not challenged.

result: SA-2 neurons are proposed to continuously monitor tissue viscoelastic state via stresses in collagen fiber strands, even in unloaded states, potentially keeping the brain updated about mechanical state of body parts and aiding motor control by updating reference frames for interpreting Type I neuron signals.
evaluation: Reviewers support these interpretations. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors have more than achieved their aims, where their results very much support the conclusions' and notes the work 'provoke[s] many further questions.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the importance and scope of the work is adequately outlined for readers to interpret the results and significance.' The functional speculation about SA-2 roles is accepted as reasonable interpretation of the data.

result: The main conclusion is that tactile neuron populations signal continuous information about the fingertip's viscoelastic deformation state shaped by both recent history and current loading. This information could potentially aid the brain in managing viscoelastic effects on tactile coding and fingertip actions, either intermittently or continuously.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly endorse the main conclusions. Reviewer 1 states 'the fundamental findings reported here provide insight into how the viscoelasticity of the fingertip skin influences the activity of mechanoreceptive afferents and thus the neural coding of force.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the authors have more than achieved their aims, where their results very much support the conclusions.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors have succeeded' and 'the results support their conclusions.'

result: The study recorded from 60 FA-1, 73 SA-1, and 41 SA-2 neurons with receptive fields distributed across the distal phalanx of 33 healthy adults. Forces mimicked natural manipulation (1.3 Hz frequency, 4N normal force, 20° tangential angles). Regular sequences had fixed trial order; irregular sequences varied preceding direction systematically. FA-2 neurons were excluded due to low responsiveness.
evaluation: Reviewers praise the methodological design. Reviewer 2 describes it as an 'elegant design of the study' with 'well designed' experiments where 'forces/displacements have been thoroughly controlled and measured to give accurate measurements.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'their study has been well designed.' The large dataset and sampling strategy are treated as strengths, with Reviewer 2 noting the 'large dataset of low threshold mechanoreceptive afferents.'

result: Background claims establish that skin is viscoelastic with deformation depending on loading history; tactile neurons signal local tissue deformations (not forces directly); fingertip properties are non-linear, viscoelastic, and anisotropic with time constants up to several seconds; and FA-1, SA-1, SA-2 neurons supply Meissner corpuscles, Merkel complexes, and Ruffini organs respectively.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these foundational claims without question. Reviewer 2 notes 'they point out in the introduction the importance of the non-linear dynamics of the event when an external stimulus contacts the skin' and states this has been 'very well-explained throughout.' The background is treated as established knowledge appropriately framing the study.

result: Discussion points include: heterogeneity between neurons is expected given distributed transduction sites and local sensitivity; mechanical anisotropy from collagen fiber orientation likely plays a crucial role; neuronal diversity might enhance population information; viscoelastic effects on task performance have not been systematically investigated; and viscoelastic memory effects may be by-products of optimization within biological constraints.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these interpretive and contextual claims. Reviewer 2 states the work will 'help us in understanding skin aging and the effects of anatomical changes of the skin better' and notes it 'provoke[s] many further questions,' indicating acceptance of the broader implications. Reviewer 3 confirms 'the importance and scope of the work is adequately outlined.'
